title: SAFEMA Tribunal Quashes Lalit Modi's FEMA Penalty in IPL 2009 South Africa Case
excerpt: The Appellate Tribunal ruled that foreign remittances for hosting IPL Season 2 in South Africa were current account transactions, overturning the Enforcement Directorate's 2018 penalties on the BCCI and its former office-bearers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • SAFEMA Tribunal quashed Lalit Modi's ₹10.65 crore penalty in IPL 2009 FEMA case on July 16.
  • BCCI's penalty reduced from ₹4 crore to ₹1 crore; other penalties also significantly cut.
  • Tribunal ruled IPL 2009 foreign remittances were current account transactions, not capital account.
  • Original penalties totaled ₹121.56 crore for transferring ₹243 crore to Cricket South Africa.
  • The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA quashed the ₹10.65 crore penalty on former IPL chairman Lalit Modi in the IPL 2009 FEMA case, in a judgment delivered on July 16.
  • BCCI's penalty was reduced from ₹4 crore to ₹1 crore; penalties on former secretary N. Srinivasan and treasurer M.P. Pandove were also cut significantly.
  • The tribunal held that the foreign remittances for staging IPL 2009 in South Africa were current account transactions — not capital account transactions — dismantling the ED's legal foundation.
  • The original ₹121.56 crore in penalties stemmed from the transfer of approximately ₹243 crore to Cricket South Africa without prior RBI approval.

Tribunal Delivers Relief After 17-Year Legal Battle

The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA has delivered a landmark verdict in the IPL 2009 FEMA violation case, providing significant relief to the BCCI and its former office-bearers. The July 16 judgment either quashed or substantially reduced the penalties that the Enforcement Directorate had imposed in May 2018 on the BCCI, former IPL chairman Lalit Modi, former secretary N. Srinivasan, and former treasurer M.P. Pandove.

The biggest beneficiary was Modi, whose entire ₹10.65 crore penalty was quashed. The tribunal called him the "chief architect behind the organization and conduct of IPL-2 in South Africa" but found he was neither responsible for BCCI's statutory FEMA compliance nor vested with the financial authority alleged by the ED.

"The penalty has been imposed even on Shri Lalit Kumar Modi in ignorance of his position and even suspension. He was not in-charge of the affairs and otherwise he has been framed in the case without any material showing his responsibility."

— SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal, July 16 judgment

Why IPL 2009 Moved to South Africa

> **"Srinivasan's New Penalty
₹5 lakh
M.P."**

The case traces to early 2009, when IPL Season 2 was moved from India to South Africa because the general elections meant state governments could not provide adequate security. The BCCI transferred USD 49.86 million (₹243.45 crore) to a Cricket South Africa account — without prior RBI approval, which the ED later alleged violated FEMA.

In May 2018, the ED imposed a combined penalty of ₹121.56 crore: ₹82.66 crore on the BCCI, ₹10.65 crore on Modi, ₹11.53 crore on Srinivasan, ₹9.72 crore on Pandove, and ₹7 crore on the State Bank of Travancore.

The Central Legal Question

The ruling hinged on a critical distinction in foreign exchange law. The ED had argued the remittances were capital account transactions requiring prior RBI approval. The tribunal found they were current account transactions related to the operational costs of staging a cricket tournament — effectively dismantling the prosecution's case.

"The Tribunal has rejected the central premise on which the Enforcement Directorate's case against me had been built. It held that the principal foreign remittances relating to the staging of IPL 2009 in South Africa were current account transactions, not capital account transactions."

— Lalit Modi

Enforcement Directorate Penalties

While Modi's penalty was entirely quashed, outcomes varied for others. BCCI's penalty dropped from ₹4 crore to ₹1 crore. Srinivasan's was cut from ₹1 crore to ₹10 lakh and Pandove's from ₹50 lakh to ₹5 lakh. In a separate set of cases, penalties of ₹50 lakh each on Srinivasan and Pandove were upheld — the tribunal finding they were "in-charge and responsible" as secretary and treasurer.

A Long Road Through the Courts

The FEMA case was one thread in a sprawling legal saga. Modi, who has lived in London since 2010, separately sought to compel the BCCI to indemnify him under Rule 34 of its by-laws. The Bombay High Court in December 2024 dismissed the petition as "frivolous and wholly misconceived," and the Supreme Court in June 2025 declined to intervene.

The tribunal's verdict noted the BCCI argued any regulatory lapse arose from "ignorance of regulatory requirements rather than mala fide intent."

What This Means for Indian Cricket

For the diaspora, the verdict closes one of the longest-running financial disputes in Indian cricket. The IPL, which Modi founded in 2007, has become one of the world's most valuable sporting properties. Modi framed the ruling as vindication: "The successful staging of that season ensured that the IPL survived and ultimately became one of the world's most valuable sporting properties."

The broader questions the case raised about regulatory compliance in cross-border sports hosting remain relevant as Indian sporting bodies increasingly look to stage events internationally.
